September 17 Board meeting record

Mayor Citrin’s Board Blames Mayor Mac’s Administration for Today’s Tax Hikes

The Records Tell a Different Story.

The official agenda described a continued discussion of a proposed Village Code amendment concerning the “prohibition of rentals of non-residential structures to the general public.” Before the meeting, David and Robin McFadden submitted detailed questions for the official record. Robin then read a statement into the record during public comment.

New · September 18
Read Mayor Mac’s Response to Mayor Citrin’s Accusations Regarding Property-Tax Increases and Infrastructure September 17 Board of Trustees meeting · Response memorandum with Exhibits A through J
View the record →

During the discussion, Deputy Mayor Michele Lindsay challenged a statement I previously submitted concerning the combined effect of rising taxes, increasing debt service, appropriated reserves, continuing infrastructure needs, and broader restrictions on private-property rights:

“Taxes are rising, debt service is increasing, reserves are being appropriated, and important infrastructure needs remain. Combining those financial pressures with broader restrictions on private-property rights risks discouraging prospective buyers, narrowing the market, and placing downward pressure on property values.”

Deputy Mayor Lindsay suggested that the current Board’s infrastructure spending and property-tax increases were necessary because my administration had deferred infrastructure work or had not raised sufficient taxes to pay for it.

Trustee Joshua Scherer then stated, in substance and not as a verbatim quotation, that he had voted to lower property taxes during my administration but, based on what he knows now, regrets that vote and would instead have voted to increase taxes.

I understood their position to be that my administration’s decision not to impose larger tax increases contributed to the Village’s present financial circumstances and forced the current Board to raise residents’ property taxes.

Deputy Mayor Lindsay asked me to submit a letter stating whether I agree that those assertions are true. I will provide that written response.

I do not agree with their characterization, and I intend to respond with the underlying financial records: budgets, tax levies, debt schedules, reserve balances, capital spending, infrastructure records, and Board minutes. In other words, I will respond with receipts.

Residents should be able to evaluate the actual documents rather than competing recollections or political assertions.

Open letter to waterfront property owners

Proposed Village laws may affect every waterfront owner and ordinary photography.

Subject: Proposed Village Laws May Affect Every Waterfront Owner and Ordinary Photography

Dear Waterfront Property Owner:

Robin and I want to make one point clear at the outset: we do not believe boathouses should be used for overnight rentals. When I served as Mayor, I led the Village's adoption of the Airbnb law intended to prevent that kind of transient lodging. We support the continued enforcement of certificate-of-occupancy, building-code, fire-safety, and short-term-rental requirements that prohibit unlawful residential use.

Our concern is different. A proposed Village law that has been described primarily as a restriction on boathouse rentals may reach much further than overnight occupancy. Read together with Chapter 51's broad and undefined restriction on photography or filming undertaken for “business or commercial gain,” the Village's approach may affect ordinary, peaceful daytime activity on private property throughout Tuxedo Park.

The proposal arose after Robin and I permitted one owner-supervised fashion photoshoot at our historic boathouse. The shoot lasted approximately six hours on a weekday and took place on the dock. There was no lodging, overnight occupancy, tenancy, public attendance, road closure, amplified sound, or transfer of possession.

Continue reading the complete letter Close the remainder of the letter

The August 19 draft expressly includes a “dock” within its definition of an accessory building. It also restricts the independent use, occupancy, rental, or leasing of accessory structures and defines compensation broadly enough to include remuneration, barter, gifts, services, loans, or other consideration.

That language creates a direct concern for every owner with a dock, whether or not the property also has a boathouse. It is not limited to our property or even to the eight separately assessed boathouses. The Village should state clearly whether it applies to every private dock on Tuxedo Lake, Wee Wah Lake, and Pond No. 3, as well as the Tuxedo Club boathouse and dock and the Village Boat Club staging area and docks.

Waterfront owners without a boathouse or dock also have reason to pay attention. The separate language of Chapter 51 concerns photography and filming throughout the Village and leaves “business or commercial gain” undefined. If the Village interprets that phrase broadly, the issue may extend beyond accessory structures to activity inside a resident's home, on a lawn or terrace, along the shoreline, or in another private or public location.

Consider a resident, guest, model, photographer, or social-media influencer who represents a clothing, jewelry, sporting-goods, design, or other product line. The person might take a photograph or short video inside a lakefront home, outside the home, on the lawn, along the shoreline, on a dock, in a boathouse, or in a public place. The content might later appear in a catalog, advertisement, website, magazine, real-estate listing, or social-media post. Compensation might consist of money, free or loaned products, travel, services, barter, commissions, sponsorship, or another benefit.

Would the Village treat that activity as prohibited or regulated commercial filming even if the owner remains present, the activity is quiet, no admission is charged, no road or public facility is occupied, and there is no measurable impact on a neighbor? Would the answer change depending on whether the image was taken in a public place, inside the person's own home, outside the home, on the shoreline, or on a dock? Would the homeowner be responsible when a guest or family member posts product-related content? The current language does not provide residents with clear answers.

This uncertainty could affect more than professional film crews. It could reach a local business owner photographing a product at home, an architect documenting completed work, a real-estate broker preparing a listing, a preservation group publishing historic images, a charity producing an appeal, the Tuxedo Club preparing promotional material, or an influencer creating a sponsored post with a mobile phone. A rule should not turn otherwise lawful, quiet conduct into a violation merely because someone involved receives compensation or a product appears in an image.

This is not a request to permit Airbnb use or overnight lodging in a boathouse. Existing certificate-of-occupancy and building-code requirements already govern residential occupancy. The concern is that a much broader law could affect peaceful daytime activities involving no lodging or rental, including photography, preservation work, professional services, real-estate marketing, charitable activity, and social use.

At the August 20 Board of Trustees meeting, I objected during public comment. During that exchange, Mayor Citrin stated that the proposed law arose from the photoshoot at our boathouse. The Village's online news archive does not currently list the recording of that meeting, so residents cannot independently review the complete exchange.

Before the Board advances this proposal, I believe residents should ask it to:

  1. Publish and preserve the complete August 20 meeting recording;
  2. State clearly whether the proposal applies to every waterfront dock on Tuxedo Lake, Wee Wah Lake, and Pond No. 3, including the Tuxedo Club boathouse and dock and the Village Boat Club staging area and docks;
  3. Explain how the Village interprets “business or commercial gain” when a resident, guest, photographer, model, or social-media influencer creates content in a public place or inside or outside a private home;
  4. Explain whether money, free or loaned products, sponsorship, commissions, barter, services, or other benefits change the Village's treatment of otherwise quiet activity;
  5. Explain the documented public-welfare problem the proposed law is intended to solve;
  6. Distinguish unlawful overnight lodging from peaceful, owner-supervised daytime activity;
  7. Evaluate the effect on separately deeded and separately assessed waterfront parcels;
  8. Create a clear safe harbor for low-impact, owner-supervised photography, filming, social, charitable, educational, professional, preservation, real-estate, and creative activity; and
  9. Use objective, impact-based standards addressing noise, traffic, parking, lighting, hours, crew size, road use, safety, and municipal services instead of a broad prohibition based primarily on compensation or content.

Please review the proposed law and supporting public record on this site. I encourage you to contact the Mayor, Trustees, John Ledwith, and the Village Clerk and ask for a clear explanation before the proposal moves forward.

Respectfully,
David and Robin McFadden
28 Pepperidge Road
Tuxedo Park, New York 10987
Owner, separately assessed boathouse at 61 Turtle Point Road

Police FOIL response received September 16

No Complaint. No Incident. No Police Record Tying the Photoshoot to a Disturbance.

The Police Department’s determination states that, after a reasonable search, it could not find records concerning the boathouse property or the single fashion photoshoot. It also found no Police Department communications concerning the property, the shoot, asserted noise, traffic, parking, safety, privacy, neighborhood-tranquility effects, or the proposed law.

What the record establishes: The Police Department reported that it found no responsive record of a complaint, call for service, incident, warning, summons, citation, or disposition concerning the boathouse photoshoot. That absence undercuts any claim that this shoot created a documented police, public-safety, or neighborhood-tranquility problem. The records do not, by themselves, establish why individual officials supported the proposed law.

An important distinction

A photoshoot listing is not a rental listing.

A professional location listing allows photographers, brands, magazines, and other clients to consider a property for a scheduled, temporary, owner-approved photography session.

Any compensation is a limited location fee. It does not provide lodging, overnight occupancy, tenancy, exclusive possession, or unrestricted access to the property.

Read Exhibit B: rental law and photoshoot distinction →
Photoshoot
  • Owner-approved and supervised
  • Temporary, scheduled activity
  • No lodging or tenancy
  • Impacts can be measured and conditioned
Residential rental
  • Occupancy of a dwelling
  • Overnight or residential use
  • Possession transferred to guests
  • Already addressed by rental regulation

Why this matters beyond one property

Property rights and financial stewardship belong in the same community conversation.

Residents already carry significant property taxes and the long-term consequences of Village spending, debt, infrastructure needs, and the use of reserves. Before adding another broad restriction, the Board should consider the cumulative effect on ownership, preservation investment, marketability, and property values.

Boathouses and docks

The proposal may reach separately assessed boathouses and docks, including facilities associated with the Tuxedo Club and other lakefront owners.

Professional and creative work

Photographers, designers, publications, real-estate professionals, and compensated social-media creators could face uncertainty under language untethered to measurable impacts.

Clubs and community institutions

Rules broad enough to reach any commercially connected image could create unintended consequences for clubs, events, publications, and promotional activity.

Every property owner

A restriction initially associated with one property establishes a rule and precedent that may later be applied to others. Clear, uniform, prospective standards protect everyone.

A reasonable alternative

Regulate actual impacts instead of imposing a categorical prohibition.

Comparable New York communities use permits, thresholds, conditions, and enforcement directed at external effects. Tuxedo Park can protect residential character while allowing peaceful, low-impact activity.

  • Limits on hours, duration, frequency, personnel, and vehicles
  • Onsite parking, insurance, and advance notice where appropriate
  • Controls for lighting, generators, traffic, noise, and public services
  • Cost recovery when extraordinary municipal services are required
  • Timely, written decisions under objective and uniformly applied standards

How to participate

Review the record and reach your own informed view.

This site is not asking anyone to sign a form letter, repeat someone else’s language, or adopt the McFaddens’ conclusions. It asks residents to examine the proposed law and source materials, consider the possible effects, and decide for themselves.

  1. Read the source materials. Begin with the waterfront-owner letter above, then examine the documents relevant to your own concerns.
  2. Review the complete draft. Consider the actual proposed language and how it would interact with the existing Village Code.
  3. Consider the practical effects. Think about privacy, safety, traffic, noise, property rights, marketability, and whether measurable impacts can be addressed through objective standards.
  4. Express your own views, if you choose. Communicate with the Board in your own words and ask that your comments be distributed and retained in the legislative record.
  5. Help others become informed. Share this site as a source of documents and competing considerations, without asking anyone to take a predetermined position.
